items.title: Finding the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle Given Its Central Angle

sections.normalized_html: The diagram above shows the unit circle. What are the coordinates of the point [MATH: P?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/aca7523739321562ee0129ca5f054028]

The diagram above shows the unit circle. What are the coordinates of the point [MATH: P?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Any point [MATH: (x,y)] on the unit circle is related to the central angle [MATH: \theta] as follows:

[MATH: x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.]

We're given that [MATH: \theta=45^\circ] at the point [MATH: P.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: x|= \cos 45^{∘} = (sqrt(2))/(2),; y|= \sin 45^{∘} = (sqrt(2))/(2).]

So, the coordinates of [MATH: P] are [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
To find the tangent of an angle using the unit circle, we need to use the relationship

Content:
[MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.]

Content:
To see why this is true, let's take a look at the following triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/18194228cf1fb1c637db5880929e639f]

Content:
For this particular triangle, we have

Content:
[MATH: \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}.]

Content:
When we take [MATH: \sin\theta] and divide it by [MATH: \cos\theta,] we get

Content:
[MATH: (\sin θ)/(\cos θ)|= (y)/(z) ÷ (x)/(z); = (y)/(z) ⋅ (z)/(x); = (y ⋅ z)/(x ⋅ z); = (y ⋅ z)/(x ⋅ z); = (y)/(x); = \tan θ.]

Content:
Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that [MATH: \tan\theta] is well-defined.

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta},] it immediately follows that

Content:
[MATH: \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}.]

The point [MATH: P\left( \dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7},\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}\right)] lies on the unit circle, as shown. What is [MATH: \tan\theta?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7}, \qquad \sin\theta =\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's consider the unit circle with a central angle [MATH: \theta] in the first quadrant, measured in the usual way.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dbd6f38c7eecfc5568af321347abd19c]

Content:
Notice that

Content:
- the [MATH: x]-coordinate of [MATH: P] coincides with the cosine of the angle [MATH: \theta,] and
- the [MATH: y]-coordinate coincides with the sine of the angle [MATH: \theta.]

Content:
So, we have
[MATH: x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.]

Content:
Consequently, if we know the angle [MATH: \theta,] we can easily work out the coordinates of the point [MATH: P,] and vice-versa. This works regardless of whether the angle [MATH: \theta] is given in degrees or radians.

Content:
For now, we'll focus on points located in the first quadrant. Later, we will encounter points in all quadrants.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle Given Its Central Angle

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/aca7523739321562ee0129ca5f054028]

The diagram above shows the unit circle. What are the coordinates of the point [MATH: P?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Any point [MATH: (x,y)] on the unit circle is related to the central angle [MATH: \theta] as follows:

[MATH: x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.]

We're given that [MATH: \theta=45^\circ] at the point [MATH: P.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: x|= \cos 45^{∘} = (sqrt(2))/(2),; y|= \sin 45^{∘} = (sqrt(2))/(2).]

So, the coordinates of [MATH: P] are [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right).]

Item 6 — Tutorial: A Proof of the Unit Circle Property

Content:
Let's consider the unit circle and a point [MATH: P(x,y)] that lies on the circle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/587cfb0adcaf4e693d6671ed2d5e5b40]

Content:
To prove that [MATH: x=\cos\theta] and [MATH: y=\sin\theta,] let's examine the triangle that's formed by [MATH: \overline{OP}] and the [MATH: x]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6c18116d1b3741038e4827a07b35d32d]

Content:
Notice that:

Content:
- The hypotenuse has length [MATH: 1] since it is a radius of the unit circle.
- The adjacent and opposite sides have lengths [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] respectively.

Content:
Therefore, using the definitions of [MATH: \cos\theta] and [MATH: \sin\theta], we have

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{1} = x, \qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{1} = y.]

Item 7 — Example: Finding a Central Angle Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle

Example Prompt:

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the point [MATH: P] is [MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2},] what is the measure of the angle [MATH: \theta?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We're given that [MATH: y=\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}] at the point [MATH: P.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: \sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.]

We compute the angle [MATH: \theta] using the inverse sine:

[MATH: \theta = \arcsin\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right) = 60^\circ.]

Item 10 — Example: Finding a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We're given that [MATH: x=\dfrac{\sqrt 8}{3}] at the point [MATH: P.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 8}{3}.]

Knowing that [MATH: \sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta},] we can calculate [MATH: \sec\theta] as follows:
[MATH: \sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 8}{3}\right)} =\dfrac{3}{\sqrt 8} = \dfrac{3\sqrt 8}{8}.]

Item 13 — Tutorial: The Relationship Between Sine, Cosine, and Tangent

Content:
To find the tangent of an angle using the unit circle, we need to use the relationship

Content:
[MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.]

Content:
To see why this is true, let's take a look at the following triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/18194228cf1fb1c637db5880929e639f]

Content:
For this particular triangle, we have

Content:
[MATH: \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}.]

Content:
When we take [MATH: \sin\theta] and divide it by [MATH: \cos\theta,] we get

Content:
[MATH: (\sin θ)/(\cos θ)|= (y)/(z) ÷ (x)/(z); = (y)/(z) ⋅ (z)/(x); = (y ⋅ z)/(x ⋅ z); = (y ⋅ z)/(x ⋅ z); = (y)/(x); = \tan θ.]

Content:
Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that [MATH: \tan\theta] is well-defined.

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta},] it immediately follows that

Content:
[MATH: \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}.]

---

Item 14 — Example: Finding the Tangent or Cotangent of a Central Angle Given a Point on the Unit Circle

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/082f1d3f6dbbf27fc349ea605979ecf7]

The point [MATH: P\left( \dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7},\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}\right)] lies on the unit circle, as shown. What is [MATH: \tan\theta?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We're given that [MATH: x=\dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7}] and [MATH: y=\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}] at the point [MATH: P.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7}, \qquad \sin\theta =\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}.]

Knowing that [MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos\theta},] we can calculate [MATH: \tan\theta] as follows:
[MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7}\right)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{42} }{\sqrt{7}} = \sqrt 6.]
